Notes

Monoplay starts with someone exhausted before the alarm has even rung and ends by returning to that exhaustion. In between, he becomes an indestructible adversary of cliques, scammers and public hypocrisy. The threats give depleted energy an outward direction, but do not deliver rest. His refusal to be readable also sits uneasily beside his demand to expose everyone else. The funeral fantasy becomes obsessively personal: even when heaven is supposed to do the punishing, he wants the credit for paying for the wreath.

chèn nào zhōng hái méi xiǎng de shí hòu zǎo diǎn shuì

早点睡 normally means going to bed early, sensible advice for a normal evening. “Before the alarm goes off” relocates it to the last scraps of a sleepless night. The everyday phrase becomes darkly comic because the opportunity to follow it has almost passed; the next insistence on continuous thinking explains why rest is so hard to reach.

  • Lyric transcript
mí cǎi fú shàng xiě shàng mí máng

Camouflage normally hides a body, but writing 'lost' across it announces the inner condition. The shared opening sound of mícǎi and mímáng makes the protective outfit disclose what it should conceal. The next line insists on wear without a recognised battlefield. Before the speaker becomes threatening, the song asks us to register a kind of damage that has no prestigious event to explain it. The return to these lines later keeps that damage underneath the boasts.

  • Genius community transcript
cāng sāng

沧桑, cāngsāng, compresses an older image of seas becoming fields: a world changed beyond recognition. It describes a person worn by experience, not only by war. Translating it as “battle-worn” catches the neighboring camouflage and battlefield, but the lyric’s point is that the wear exists even without the recognized event that would explain it.

  • Ministry of Education: 滄桑
  • Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 滄海桑田
  • Lyric text
jǐ zhuī

The spine supplies a hard, upright center after exhaustion, camouflage and unseen enemies. An indestructible backbone is a bodily boast, but its placement also reads as the determination not to bend. The song moves from being worn out to imagining a part of the self that cannot be made weak, preparing the turn from inward fatigue to outward attack.

  • Lyric transcript
fèi le nǐ men de zuǐ

The opening’s 废 describes feeling useless or spent; 废了 here becomes something the speaker will do to other people’s mouths—ruin or disable them. The shared word converts a state of personal depletion into an outward threat, still directed at speech rather than an identified opponent.

  • Lyric text
bào tuán qǔ nuǎn

He attacks closed circles that protect their own, yet later speaks tenderly of how rough his brothers have it. The target is therefore not companionship in itself. It is solidarity that shields deception or keeps outsiders powerless. That distinction gives the anti-clique anger more substance than a blanket claim to need nobody. The song wants a 'we' capable of surviving dirty conditions without becoming the self-protecting group it condemns.

  • Genius community transcript
wǒ yě shì zuì le

我也是醉了, literally “I’m drunk too,” became a conversational expression of exasperation or disbelief: the equivalent of “I can’t even.” It lets the speaker react to something absurd by describing his own helplessness. In a verse opened by fatigue, the stock joke briefly returns the aggressive voice to being overwhelmed.

  • Lyric text
dà fù wēng

大富翁 is both a very wealthy person and the name of property-and-money games, including the Richman series. The next line brings in anti-addiction language, activating the game association. The title “Monoplay” fits that field of play without naming a particular game. Wealth and competitive absorption sit together, making accumulation look like a pastime someone cannot stop.

  • SOFTSTAR: Richman 4 official game description
  • Lyric text
fáng chén mí

防沉迷, fáng chénmí, is familiar from systems intended to limit excessive online gaming, including official rules for minors. It is not a new legal idea waiting to be invented. Following 大富翁, the phrase gives the verse’s rich people or game players the vocabulary of a monitored habit, turning accumulation into something that might need an enforced stopping point.

  • National Press and Publication Administration: anti-addiction gaming notice (2021)
  • Lyric transcript
hǎi jiāo

海椒, hǎijiāo, is a regional word for chili used in Sichuan and neighboring areas. “Chili” gets the ingredient across but loses the local voice. Placing it beside kangaroo meat makes a comic meeting of the distant and familiar: an unusual food is approached with the everyday seasoning vocabulary of home.

  • Linguistic study: regional words for chili peppers
  • Genius community transcript
zì hāi guō

自嗨锅 is the Zihaiguo self-heating meal brand. 自嗨, zìhāi, also means entertaining oneself or getting excited inside one’s own bubble. Calling the meal expired makes a shelf-life judgment double as a judgment on self-absorption. Coming after the little cliques, the convenience-food label becomes a compact joke about people impressed chiefly by themselves.

  • Zihaiguo official website
  • Lyric text
wú lài

无赖 can describe a shameless rogue who refuses ordinary obligations or reasoning. After condemning cliques and deception, the speaker claims the disreputable label for himself. That removes one weapon from opponents: threatening his respectability has less force if he has already theatrically thrown it away. The laugh that follows enjoys that freedom.

  • Lyric transcript
tiān zì rán huì shōu nǐ

天, heaven, acts as the eventual enforcer; 收 makes the person sound ready to be taken away or collected. Repeating this after “I don’t even have to touch you” imagines revenge without direct effort. It reprises “Cube,” where the speaker also hands punishment upward, before returning here to meticulously personalized threats.

  • Lyric transcript
biàn sè lóng

He celebrates being impossible to see through, then threatens to tear away somebody else's respectable cover in public. The asymmetry is revealing: concealment is protection when it belongs to him, hypocrisy when it belongs to an adversary. The song need not be a consistent moral code for this to matter. It stages the demands of a cornered person who wants control over his own exposure and over the exposure of those he distrusts.

  • Lyric transcript
é měng

蛾蠓 names the tiny moth-like flies associated with damp drains. After the chameleon and a threat to blind the listener, this thoroughly unglamorous bathroom insect brings the menace close to everyday life. The image does not need a large predator: something small, intrusive and difficult to ignore can already make an ordinary room unpleasant.

  • Lyric transcript
qí pā

奇葩 originally names an extraordinary flower, but conversationally it often describes a bizarre person or thing. “Freak” selects that latter force. The speaker embraces the label and places himself in another world, then immediately asks whether the listener is afraid to go home. His strangeness crosses from self-description into the listener’s most familiar space.

  • Lyric transcript
yǎn jiǎng tái

A podium gives someone a height, an audience and a claim to authority. The threat is to expose that person in front of children until the audience laughs. It mirrors “Sunshine” by turning an instructional setting against its authoritative figure: the person who expects everyone to listen becomes the object everybody watches.

  • Lyric transcript
zhē xiū bù

遮羞布 literally means a cloth covering shame, figuratively the respectable excuse or appearance hiding something disgraceful. English “fig leaf” replaces the material image with an equivalent idiom. Tearing it away on a podium turns exposure into a public event: the person’s authority collapses not through a counterargument, but through becoming laughable before the audience.

  • Lyric text
hái néng hū xī

Muddy water makes seeing difficult, but the line answers with the ability to breathe. That shift changes the stakes from judging appearances to remaining alive within a hostile environment. The plural “we” briefly breaks the isolated self-mythology: the following lament for “my brothers” makes survival a shared condition, not only a personal boast.

  • Lyric transcript
tōu jiān shuǎ huá

偷奸耍滑 describes using sly tricks to avoid effort or responsibility. It is not the same as the outright fraud in the parallel line about scams. Keeping the two accusations distinct makes the repeated contempt target both active deception and opportunistic evasion.

  • Lyric text
shàng fén de lù shàng

上坟 means visiting a grave to pay respects, rather than simply being buried. The line bends that ordinary ritual journey into an ambush-like meeting place. After saying there is a long road ahead, the speaker supplies a destination that cancels the other person’s future; the wreath and payment details then turn the imagined aftermath into a carefully managed event.

  • Lyric transcript
gāo gē bù duàn měng jìn

高歌 and 猛进 recall the heroic idiom 高歌猛进, advancing vigorously while singing. In this funeral-bound sequence, the triumphant movement is grotesquely misplaced. A phrase suited to confidence and collective progress carries someone toward the grave scene instead, continuing the song’s habit of turning positive public language into a private taunt.

  • Lyric transcript
qián shì wǒ chū de

The repeated correction about who paid is smaller and more personal than the grand threat of death. Even the enemy's supposed tribute from loved ones turns out to depend on the speaker. He wants authorship of the humiliation, not merely justice arriving by itself. That undermines the repeated claim that heaven can handle everything without his involvement. When exhaustion returns afterwards, the elaborate fantasy has not freed him from the conflict.

  • Genius community transcript

About Jackzebra and this mixtape

Zhuang Zhuang Mixtape arrived on Surf Gang on October 2, 2026: 55 tracks, opening with Sour and closing with Sweet. Its cast widens from YoungQueenz on Poker Face to User116, Effie, kuru, yoyi, 春 and 南部犯罪份子. Aghast has a production credit on every track from Hitman through Snatch, giving that stretch a shared collaborator behind its changing scenes.

Surf Gang release · Artist credits

Jackzebra told AVYSS that he writes while singing over a beat he has listened to repeatedly, keeping the images in his head central. He values the room Mandarin leaves for indirect meanings. Listen for ordinary phrases becoming physical scenes: familiarity becomes cooking, authority becomes family seniority, and a tired saying suddenly turns into a threat.

AVYSS interview, 2024

In STATIC, he describes mixtapes as a format for letting ideas flow, reserving an official debut album for later. In a separate conversation about Above & Beyond, he compared that earlier tape to a collection of his producer friends’ work. The credits here likewise reward attention: long-running collaborators sit alongside guests working in Mandarin, Korean and English.

STATIC interview · Sabukaru interview, 2025

The small details connect to his stated interests: he has described playing Temple Run in transit and before shows, watching Top Boy, and wanting to score White Oleander. These give the songs specific points of contact with his life. The notes follow those connections alongside the lyrics’ jokes, invented scenes and competing voices.

His recommendations in Perfectly Imperfect · Dazed interview, 2025 · Interview questionnaire, 2025

Jackzebra has pushed back on being made to represent all of China’s underground. These notes stay close to the words: what an expression usually means, what changes in this line, and how another song answers it. Cultural references have sources; interpretations rest on details you can hear or read in the song.
